Calculus.description: Calculus (dental tartar) is hardened dental plaque that has calcified on the surfaces of teeth. It forms when mineral salts from saliva combine with plaque bacteria, creating a rock-hard deposit that cannot be removed by brushing alone.
symptoms: Yellow or brown deposits on teeth near the gum line
Rough or gritty texture on tooth surfaces
Persistent bad breath (halitosis)
Swollen, red, or bleeding gums
Receding gum line
causes: Poor oral hygiene and infrequent brushing
Consuming sugary or starchy foods frequently
prevention: Brush teeth at least twice daily with fluoride toothpaste
Floss daily to remove plaque between teeth
Visit a dentist every 6 months for professional cleaning
Drink plenty of water throughout the day
treatment: Professional dental scaling and root planing
Ultrasonic scaling devices used by dentists
Prescription antimicrobial mouthwash in severe cases

Caries.description: Dental caries (tooth decay) is a bacterial disease that destroys the hard tissues of the tooth — enamel, dentine, and cementum. It is one of the most prevalent chronic diseases worldwide, caused by acid produced by bacteria that ferment dietary sugars.
symptoms: Toothache or spontaneous tooth pain
Tooth sensitivity to hot, cold, or sweet foods
Visible holes or pits in teeth
Brown, black, or white staining on tooth surfaces
Pain when biting down
causes: Frequent consumption of sugary or acidic foods and drinks
Poor oral hygiene — inadequate brushing and flossing
Dry mouth reducing saliva's protective effect
Deep tooth grooves that trap food particles
prevention: Brush twice daily with fluoride toothpaste
Limit sugary snacks and acidic beverages
Regular dental check-ups and fluoride treatments
treatment: Root canal treatment for infection reaching pulp
Tooth extraction as a last resort

Gingivitis.description: Gingivitis is inflammation of the gums (gingiva) caused by bacterial plaque accumulation at the gum line. It is the earliest stage of gum disease and is reversible with proper treatment and improved oral hygiene.
symptoms: Red, swollen, or puffy gums
Gums that bleed easily during brushing or flossing
Bad breath (halitosis)
Receding gums
Tender gums when touched
causes: Plaque buildup on teeth and gum line
Certain medications that affect gum tissue
prevention: Maintain a balanced diet rich in vitamins

Tooth Discoloration.description: Tooth discoloration refers to staining, yellowing, or abnormal pigmentation of the teeth. It can affect the outer surface (extrinsic) or be embedded within the tooth structure (intrinsic), and ranges from minor cosmetic concerns to indicators of systemic conditions.
symptoms: Yellowing or browning of tooth surfaces
White spots or streaks on enamel
Grey or dark patches on teeth
Uneven coloring across different teeth
Surface stains that do not respond to brushing
causes: Consumption of staining foods and drinks (coffee, tea, red wine)
Poor oral hygiene allowing plaque and tartar buildup
Aging — natural thinning of enamel revealing yellow dentin
Trauma or injury to the tooth
prevention: Limit intake of staining beverages; use a straw
Rinse mouth with water after consuming staining foods
treatment: Dental polishing to remove surface stains
Addressing underlying causes (medication changes, fluoride management)

Ulcers.description: Oral ulcers (aphthous ulcers or canker sores) are painful, open sores that develop on the mucous membranes inside the mouth. They can appear on the inside of the cheeks, lips, tongue, gums, or throat, causing significant discomfort when eating or speaking.
symptoms: Round or oval white or yellow sores with a red border
Painful, burning sensation in the mouth
Difficulty eating, drinking, or speaking
Swollen lymph nodes in severe cases
Fever (in complex aphthous ulcers)
causes: Minor mouth injuries from dental work or accidental biting
Immune system disorders or inflammatory conditions
prevention: Ensure adequate nutrition (B vitamins, zinc, iron)
treatment: Prescription medication for severe or recurrent cases

Hypodontia.description: Hypodontia is the congenital absence of one or more teeth (excluding third molars/wisdom teeth). It is the most common dental developmental anomaly, affecting tooth development during the embryonic stage. It can affect both primary and permanent dentition.
symptoms: Missing teeth with no signs of previous extraction
Gaps in the dental arch
Abnormal spacing between existing teeth
Retained primary (baby) teeth due to missing permanent successors
Shifted or drifted adjacent teeth
causes: Evolutionary tooth size and number reduction
Down syndrome or other chromosomal conditions
prevention: Hypodontia cannot be fully prevented as it is primarily genetic
Regular dental monitoring from early childhood
Genetic counseling for families with history
Protecting remaining teeth from decay and trauma
treatment: Dental implants to replace missing teeth
Dental bridges supported by adjacent teeth
Orthodontic treatment to close or manage gaps
Composite resin build-ups on retained primary teeth
